claims.text: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy has a fine lamellar FCC/B2 dual-phase microstructure.
Internal boundaries in the lamellar colonies serve as microcrack-nucleation sites during room-temperature tensile loading.
Microcracking along internal colony boundaries causes brittle failure and limited tensile ductility in the baseline alloy.
Warm forging at approximately 800–900 °C can be conducted below the alloy's full recrystallization temperature.
Warm forging at 800–900 °C promotes plastic flow in the eutectic alloy.
The proposed warm-forging treatment slightly reduces inter-lamellar spacing.
Warm forging followed by a short sub-critical anneal partially spheroidizes and refines the lamellar interfaces.
The sub-critical anneal stabilizes the refined lamellar structure produced by forging.
The modified interface structure enhances dislocation transmission across lamellae.
Greater lamellar deformability or dislocation transmission can alleviate local stress concentrations rather than create cracks.
Partial spheroidization and refinement of the interfaces reduce stress concentrations within the lamellar colonies.
Reduced interfacial stress concentrations suppress premature microcrack initiation and propagation.
The treatment increases tensile strength through dislocation-based strengthening.
The treatment improves room-temperature elongation by mitigating premature interfacial failure.
The treated alloy will have at least a 20% higher ultimate tensile strength than the untreated as-cast baseline.
The treated alloy will have at least a 10% higher elongation at fracture than the untreated as-cast baseline.
Excessive treatment temperature or annealing time can over-coarsen the microstructure and negate the benefits of refinement.
The magnitude of the strength and ductility changes depends on the thermal cycle and initial microstructure.
